citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

derivations.claim: [Self-adjointness of $K$] The function $\kappa$ is real, measurable and finite-valued, so $M_\kappa$ is self-adjoint on $D(M_\kappa)=\{v:\kappa v\in L^2\}$ by [F1]; conjugating by the unitary $\mathcal F_2$ ([F1]) gives that $K=\mathcal F_2^*M_\kappa\mathcal F_2$ is self-adjoint with $D(K)=\mathcal F_2^{-1}D(M_\kappa)=\{u:\kappa\mathcal F_2u\in L^2\}$ ([F2]). For $u\in D(K)$, $\langle Ku,u\rangle=\langle M_\kappa\mathcal F_2u,\mathcal F_2u\rangle=\int\kappa|\mathcal F_2u|^2\ge0$, so $K\ge0$.

[Finitely many components] Let $\mathfrak K_1,\dots,\mathfrak K_r$ be Hilbert spaces and let $T_a$ be self-adjoint on $\mathfrak K_a$ for $a=1,\dots,r$. On the direct sum $\bigoplus_a\mathfrak K_a$ with domain $\{(u_a):u_a\in D(T_a)\}$ define $T((u_a)):=(T_au_a)$. Then $T$ is symmetric (componentwise), and if $(u^{(k)})$ is in the domain with $u^{(k)}\to u$ and $Tu^{(k)}\to\eta$, then componentwise $u_a^{(k)}\to u_a$ and $T_au_a^{(k)}\to\eta_a$; closedness of $T_a$ gives $u_a\in D(T_a)$, $T_au_a=\eta_a$ and $\sum_a\|T_au_a\|^2=\|\eta\|^2<\infty$, so $T$ is closed. Testing the adjoint componentwise shows $D(T^*)=D(T)$ and $T^*=T$; a symmetric densely defined operator whose adjoint has the same domain is self-adjoint. If all $T_a=T_0$ and $\mathfrak K_a=\mathfrak K_0$, then $T\ge-\|V\|_\infty$ whenever $T_0\ge-\|V\|_\infty$, because the quadratic form is the sum of the components.

[Identification with $W^{2,2}$ and the core] For $\xi\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ one has $c_{\min}(1+|\xi|^2)\le 1+\kappa(\xi)\le c_{\max}(1+|\xi|^2)$ for suitable positive constants $c_{\min},c_{\max}$ depending only on $N,m_i,\hbar$; hence $\kappa\mathcal F_2u\in L^2$ if and only if $(1+|\xi|^2)\mathcal F_2u\in L^2$, i.e. $u\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$, with equivalent norms by [F3]. Since $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $W^{2,2}$ ([F3]) and the graph norm of $K$ is equivalent to the $W^{2,2}$ norm, $C_c^\infty$ is a core for $K$, and $K$ is the unique self-adjoint extension of $K|_{C_c^\infty}$ ([F5]).

[Bounded perturbation] Since $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$, the operator $M_V$ is bounded with $\|M_V\|\le\|V\|_\infty$; it is symmetric as multiplication by a real function, and on $D(K)$ the bound $\|M_Vu\|\le 0\cdot\|Ku\|+\|V\|_\infty\|u\|$ exhibits the admissible pair $(a,b)=(0,\|V\|_\infty)$. By [F4] with $A=K$ and $\gamma=0$, $H=K+M_V$ is self-adjoint on $D(K)$ and bounded below by $-\|V\|_\infty$. Moreover $\|Hu\|\le\|Ku\|+\|V\|_\infty\|u\|$ and $\|Ku\|\le\|Hu\|+\|V\|_\infty\|u\|$, so the graph norms of $H$ and $K$ are equivalent on $D(K)$; hence the core $C_c^\infty$ of step 2.1 is also a core for $H$. This proves (a) and (b).

[The scalar case with $r$ components] The Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)\otimes\mathbb C^r$ is identified with $\bigoplus_{a=1}^rL^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$ componentwise; under this identification $K\otimes I_r+M_V\otimes I_r$ is the direct sum of $r$ copies of $H$ with domain $D(K)^{\oplus r}=D(K)\otimes\mathbb C^r$. By step 3.1 and step 1.2 it is self-adjoint and bounded below by $-\|V\|_\infty$, which is (c).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1-3.1 prove (a), (b) and (c); the displayed reduction for external and pair potentials only uses the triangle inequality for essential suprema, $\|V\|_\infty\le\sum_i\|V_i\|_\infty+\sum_{i<j}\|W_{ij}\|_\infty<\infty$. No HVZ threshold, stability, thermodynamic-limit or physical-interpretation claim is made.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
including $n=0$, a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given (so $T_0$ is a
self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb C$),
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

(a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded
linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with
$$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies
$\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$,
$\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$
on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$,
and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear.

(b) *Creation and annihilation on the core.* Define, for $f\in H$ and
$\psi\in F_0$,
$$(S_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\quad (S_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$(S_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\ (n\ge0).$$
Then $S_+(f)\psi,S_-(f)\psi\in F_0$; $S_+(f)$ is linear in $f$ and
$S_-(f)$ is conjugate-linear in $f$; and with
$\|\psi\|_1^2:=\sum_{n}\bigl(n+1\bigr)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for $\psi\in F_0$,
$$\|S_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1,\qquad \|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$

(c) *Adjoint relation.* $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S_-(f)\psi\rangle$
for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$
([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$,
$$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$
and consequently
$$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$

Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no
physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a linear
operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$ and graph $\Gamma(T)$
([[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]).

$T$ is **densely defined** when $D(T)$ is a dense subset of $H$
([[def-dense-top]]); **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of
$H\oplus H$; and **closable** when $T$ has a closed extension.
Recall that the graph norm is $\|x\|_T=(\|x\|^2+\|Tx\|^2)^{1/2}$.

**The graph-norm dictionary.** The following three statements are part of the
definition's content and are proved in the remarks below rather than assumed:

1. $\|\cdot\|_T$ is a norm on $D(T)$, and
   $x\mapsto(x,Tx)$ is an isometric isomorphism of $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ onto
   $\Gamma(T)$;
2. $T$ is closed if and only if $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$ is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
3. if $T$ is closed, then $D(T)$ is a Hilbert space for the inner product
   $\langle x,y\rangle_T=\langle x,y\rangle+\langle Tx,Ty\rangle$ whose induced
   norm is $\|\cdot\|_T$.

A linear subspace $D_0\subseteq D(T)$ is a **core** for a closed operator $T$
when $D_0$ is dense in $(D(T),\|\cdot\|_T)$, equivalently when
$\overline{\Gamma(T|_{D_0})}=\Gamma(T)$, where the closure is taken in
$H\oplus H$ and $T|_{D_0}$ denotes the restriction of $T$ to $D_0$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: [The raising operator and its closure] For every $n$ the map $\psi\mapsto P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)$ is bounded with norm at most $\|f\|$ by [F2], so $D(A_+(f))$ is a linear subspace containing $F_0$ and $A_+(f)$ is a linear operator extending $S_+(f)$ with $(A_+(f)\psi)_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for all $\psi\in D(A_+(f))$ and $\sum_n\|(A_+(f)\psi)_n\|^2<\infty$, so $A_+(f)\psi\in F(H)$. If $\psi^{(k)}\in D(A_+(f))$ with $\psi^{(k)}\to\psi$ and $A_+(f)\psi^{(k)}\to\eta$, then for each $m\ge1$ continuity of $\psi\mapsto P_+^{(m)}(f\otimes\psi_{m-1})$ gives $\eta_m=\sqrt mP_+^{(m)}(f\otimes\psi_{m-1})$, and $\eta_0=0$. For every finite $N$, continuity of the norm and the finite sum gives $$\sum_{n=0}^N(n+1)\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\|^2=\lim_k\sum_{n=0}^N(n+1)\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n^{(k)})\|^2\le\lim_k\|A_+(f)\psi^{(k)}\|^2=\|\eta\|^2.$$ Taking the supremum over $N$ shows $\psi\in D(A_+(f))$; the coordinate formulas then give $A_+(f)\psi=\eta$, so $A_+(f)$ is closed. For $\psi\in D(A_+(f))$ the truncations $\psi^{(N)}$ lie in $F_0$, satisfy $\psi^{(N)}\to\psi$, and $A_+(f)\psi^{(N)}\to A_+(f)\psi$ because the defining series of $\psi$ converges; hence $F_0$ is a core and $A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}$.

[The lowering operator is the core adjoint] For $\psi\in F(H)$ set $\eta_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}\psi_{n+1}$. For $\varphi\in F_0$, [F2] gives $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\sum_{n\ge0}\langle\varphi_n,\eta_n\rangle$, a finite sum because $\varphi$ has finite support. If $\sum_n\|\eta_n\|^2<\infty$, Cauchy--Schwarz shows this functional is bounded on $F_0$ and its representing vector is $(\eta_n)_n=A_-(f)\psi$. Conversely, if the functional is bounded with norm $C$, let $\varphi^{(N)}$ have coordinates $\eta_n$ for $n\le N$ and zero thereafter. Then $\varphi^{(N)}\in F_0$ and $S_N:=\sum_{n\le N}\|\eta_n\|^2=|\langle S_+(f)\varphi^{(N)},\psi\rangle|\le C\|\varphi^{(N)}\|=C\sqrt{S_N}$, so $S_N\le C^2$ for every $N$. Hence $(\eta_n)_n\in F(H)$ and the functional is represented by $A_-(f)\psi$. Thus $\psi\in D(S_+(f)^*)$ exactly when $\sum_n(n+1)\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\psi_{n+1}\|^2<\infty$, and $S_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$. As an adjoint $A_-(f)$ is closed, and it is densely defined because it contains $F_0$.

[Weighted domain and bounds] For $\psi\in D_1$, $\sum_n(n+1)\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\|^2\le\|f\|^2\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ and likewise $\sum_n(n+1)\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\|^2\le\|f\|^2\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_{n+1}\|^2<\infty$, so $D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$ and the bounds of (c) follow from the same estimates; since $F_0\subseteq D_1$, this also gives the density in (b).

[Mutual adjoints] Since $A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_+(f)^{**}$ by step 1.1, [F3] gives $A_+(f)^*=S_+(f)^{***}=S_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$ by step 1.2. Applying the same step 1.2 with the roles of $S_+$ and $S_-$ exchanged (the adjoint relation of [F2] is symmetric in the two core operators) gives $S_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$, hence $A_-(f)^*=S_+(f)^{**}=A_+(f)$. Consequently both operators are closed with the stated adjoint pairs, proving (a) and (b) apart from the domain inclusion.

[The weighted norm identity] Let $\psi\in D_1$ and let $\psi^{(N)}$ be its truncations; then $\psi^{(N)}\to\psi$ and, by the sector formulas and the convergence of the defining sums of $\psi$, $A_\pm(g)\psi^{(N)}\to A_\pm(g)\psi$. The identity of [[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]] (d) applies to $\psi^{(N)}\in F_0$; passing to the limit in $\|A_+(g)\psi^{(N)}\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi^{(N)}\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi^{(N)}\|^2$ using continuity of the norm and of addition in $F(H)$ gives the displayed identity for $\psi$. This proves (d) and completes the proof.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
including $n=0$, a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given (so $T_0$ is a
self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb C$),
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$ and symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]], so that
$$F(H)=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)},\ \sum_n\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}$$
is a Hilbert space. For $n\in\mathbb N$ define
$$\Pi_n:F(H)\to F(H),\qquad \Pi_n\psi:=(0,\dots,0,\psi_n,0,\dots)$$
(the entry $\psi_n$ in coordinate $n$ and $0$ in all other coordinates). Then:

(a) each $\Pi_n$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|\Pi_n\psi\|=\|\psi_n\|$ and $\|\Pi_n\|\le1$; it satisfies
$\Pi_n^2=\Pi_n$, $\Pi_n^*=\Pi_n$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]), and
$\Pi_n$ is the Hilbert orthogonal projection of $F(H)$ onto the closed subspace
$\iota_n(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)})$ of vectors supported in coordinate $n$
([[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]]);

(b) $\Pi_n\Pi_m=0$ for $n\ne m$, so the ranges are pairwise orthogonal and
$\|\Pi_n\|=1$ whenever $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ne\{0\}$ (which holds for
every $n$ when $H\ne\{0\}$);

(c) for every $\psi\in F(H)$ the series $\sum_{n}\Pi_n\psi$ converges in norm to
$\psi$, the expansion is orthogonal,
$$\psi=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\Pi_n\psi,\qquad \|\psi\|^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\Pi_n\psi\|^2,$$
and the partial sums $\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n$ converge to the identity in the strong
operator topology, i.e. $\bigl\|\psi-\sum_{n\le N}\Pi_n\psi\bigr\|\to0$ for
every $\psi\in F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]);

(d) $\Pi_n=0$ as an operator if and only if
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\{0\}$; for $H\ne\{0\}$ no $\Pi_n$ vanishes.

No physical interpretation of the Fock space or of its sectors is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be an orthonormal basis of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$,
that is, a complete orthonormal family
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]), and
define the **Fourier coefficient map**

$$\Phi:H\to\ell^2(I,\mathbb F),\qquad \Phi(x):=(\langle x,e_i\rangle)_{i\in I}$$with values in the space of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Then $\Phi$ is a linear bijection satisfying$$\|\Phi(x)\|_2=\|x\|,\qquad \langle \Phi(x),\Phi(y)\rangle_{\ell^2}=\langle x,y\rangle \qquad\text{for all } x,y\in H .$$

In particular $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete, hence a Hilbert space, with
the inner product of [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field and let
$T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) whose range $T(X)$ admits an ordered basis of
finite length ([[def-linear-basis]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space, let $Y$ be a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]), and let
$T_n:X\to Y$, $n\in\mathbb N$, be compact operators
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) with $\|T_n-T\|\to0$ for a bounded linear
operator $T:X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]],
[[def-operator-norm]], [[def-metric-convergence]]). Then $T$ is compact.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and $K$
be Hilbert spaces over the same real or complex scalar field and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is trace class
([[def-trace-class-operator]]) if and only if there are families
$(u_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $H$ and $(v_j)_{j\ge1}$ in $K$, indexed by the positive
integers, with
$$\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<+\infty$$
such that the zero-based sequence of finite-rank operators defined by $R_0=0$
and
$$R_m:=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle\cdot,u_j\rangle v_j\qquad(m\ge1)$$
converges to $T$ in operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]],
[[def-metric-convergence]]).  Here the displayed scalar series is, under the
library convention, the series of the sequence
$(\|u_{m+1}\|\,\|v_{m+1}\|)_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case
$$\|T\|_1=\inf\Bigl\{\sum_{j\ge1}\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|:\ R_m\to T\ \text{in operator norm}\Bigr\},$$
the infimum being over all such **nuclear representations** of $T$, with the
same zero-based shift understood in every displayed sum, and the
infimum is attained: using its positive-integer index set and padding finite rank by zeros,
the singular-value series
$T=\sum_{j\in J}s_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ is a nuclear representation with
sum $\|T\|_1$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For every double sequence $(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb N}$ in $[0,+\infty]$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right)=\sup_{m,n\in\mathbb N}\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right),$$

where every sum is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Thus the order of summation may be interchanged, even when the common value is $+\infty$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $S$ is bounded
   above ([[def-bounded-set]]), then $(x_k)$ converges ([[def-real-limit]]) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) supplies the
first and [[thm-infimum-property]] the second, and each is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

derivations.claim: [Orthonormality] Let $I=(j_1\le\cdots\le j_n)$, $I'=(j'_1\le\cdots\le j'_m)$ and first suppose $n=m\ge1$. Using $P_+^{(n)}=P_+^{(n)*}$ and $P_+^{(n)}\chi=\chi$ for $\chi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, [F2] gives $\langle v_I,v_{I'}\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\langle e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n},U_\pi(e_{j'_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j'_n})\rangle$. Each summand is $1$ exactly when $\pi$ maps the tuple $(j'_1,\dots,j'_n)$ to $(j_1,\dots,j_n)$ and $0$ otherwise, by orthonormality of the $e_j$; since both tuples are nondecreasing, such $\pi$ exists only if $I=I'$, and then the number of such $\pi$ is the product of the factorials of the multiplicities of $I$. Hence $\langle v_I,v_{I'}\rangle=0$ for $I\ne I'$ and $\|v_I\|^2\ge1/n!>0$, so $(u_I)$ is an orthonormal family; tensors from different $n$ are orthogonal by [F1].

[Factoring the finite sums] Fix $N\ge1$. The map $I\mapsto(n_1,\dots,n_N)$ assigning to a multiset $I\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}$ the number $n_j$ of occurrences of $j$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb N^N$, and $\lambda_I=\sum_jn_j\varepsilon_j$; by [F5] and the geometric series with $q=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}\in(0,1)$, $\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}}e^{-\beta\lambda_I}=\sum_{(n_1,\dots,n_N)\in\mathbb N^N}\prod_{j=1}^N e^{-\beta n_j\varepsilon_j}=\prod_{j=1}^N\sum_{n\ge0}e^{-\beta n\varepsilon_j}=\prod_{j=1}^N\frac1{1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}}$, the interchange of the finite product with the sums following by induction from [F5] (Tonelli for nonnegative series).

[Completeness] The ordered elementary tensors $e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n}$ have dense span in $H^{\otimes n}$ ([F2]); applying the bounded projection $P_+^{(n)}$ gives a dense subset of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and the vectors $P_+^{(n)}(e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n})$ over ordered tuples coincide with those over nondecreasing tuples because $P_+^{(n)}U_\pi=P_+^{(n)}$ ([F2]). Hence the span of $\{u_I:|I|=n\}$ is dense in $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$; combining the sectors and using that every $\psi\in F(H)$ is the limit of its truncations ([F1]) shows that the span of all $u_I$ is dense in $F(H)$. With step 1.1 this proves (a).

[The infinite product and the criterion] The finite sums of step 1.2 increase with $N$ because all terms are positive, and every finite multiset $I$ lies in an initial segment, so $\sum_{I\in\mathcal M}e^{-\beta\lambda_I}=\lim_N\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}}e^{-\beta\lambda_I}=\lim_N\prod_{j\le N}(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j})^{-1}\in(0,\infty]$. Put $q_j=e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}\in(0,1)$. For every $j$, [F6] gives $q_j\le-\log(1-q_j)\le q_j/(1-q_j)$. If infinitely many $q_j>1/2$, both $\sum_jq_j$ and $\sum_j-\log(1-q_j)$ diverge, the latter already bounded below by the former termwise. Otherwise only finitely many such terms occur, all finite, and on the remaining tail $q_j\le-\log(1-q_j)\le2q_j$; therefore the logarithmic sum is finite exactly when $\sum_jq_j$ is finite. By the product and reciprocal laws in [F7], $\log\prod_{j\le N}(1-q_j)^{-1}=\sum_{j\le N}-\log(1-q_j)$. If these logarithmic partial sums are bounded, the increasing reciprocal products are bounded as well, since $\log$ is increasing and $\exp$ is its increasing inverse; hence [F8] gives a finite limit. Conversely, if the reciprocal products have a finite limit, they are bounded and [F7] makes their logarithmic partial sums bounded. In the finite case, if $P_N$ denotes the reciprocal partial product and $P_N\to P$, continuity of $\log$ gives $\log P=\sum_j-\log(1-q_j)$, so $P=\exp(\sum_j-\log(1-q_j))$. This proves (c) and (d) in both large-factor branches without assuming summability in advance.

[The diagonal operator and the $\mathcal M$-indexed trace criterion] By step 2.1 and [F3], the diagonal operator $D_\beta$ is self-adjoint; Parseval from [F4] gives $\|D_\beta\psi\|^2=\sum_I\mu_I^2|\langle\psi,u_I\rangle|^2\le\|\psi\|^2$, so its domain is all of $F(H)$ and it is bounded with norm at most one. Its coefficients are positive, so $\langle D_\beta\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_I\mu_I|\langle\psi,u_I\rangle|^2\ge0$; hence it is positive. The set $\mathcal M$ is countably infinite: group its finite nondecreasing sequences by the integer $n+\sum_{r=1}^n j_r$, list each finite group lexicographically, skip empty groups, and concatenate the groups (the singleton sequences ensure infinitely many entries). Fix the resulting enumeration $I_1,I_2,\ldots$ and put $\mu_m:=e^{-\beta\lambda_{I_m}}$. If $\sum_I\mu_I<\infty$, define $R_N\psi:=\sum_{m=1}^N\mu_m\langle\psi,u_{I_m}\rangle u_{I_m}$. Each $R_N$ is finite rank and compact by [F4], while Parseval gives $\|D_\beta-R_N\|\le\sup_{m>N}\mu_m\le\sum_{m>N}\mu_m\to0$. Thus $D_\beta$ is compact by [F4]. Its coefficient expansion is the nuclear representation $D_\beta\psi=\sum_{m\ge1}\langle\psi,u_{I_m}\rangle(\mu_m u_{I_m})$, whose nuclear sum is $\sum_m\mu_m<\infty$; [F4] therefore proves that $D_\beta$ is trace class. Conversely, if $D_\beta$ is trace class, [F9] applied to the supplied basis $(u_I)$ gives $\operatorname{tr}D_\beta=\sum_I\langle D_\beta u_I,u_I\rangle=\sum_I\mu_I<\infty$. Hence $D_\beta$ is trace class exactly when the $\mathcal M$-indexed sum is finite, and then its trace is that sum.

[Conclusion] Combining step 3.1 with step 2.2 gives (e): $D_\beta$ is trace class if and only if $\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$, and then $\operatorname{tr}D_\beta=\sum_Ie^{-\beta\lambda_I}=\prod_{j\ge1}(1-e^{-\beta\varepsilon_j})^{-1}$. Parts (a)-(e) are proved, and no thermal or measurement interpretation is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

(a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded
linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with
$$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies
$\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$,
$\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$
on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$,
and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear.

(b) *Creation and annihilation on the core.* Define, for $f\in H$ and
$\psi\in F_0$,
$$(S_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\quad (S_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$(S_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\ (n\ge0).$$
Then $S_+(f)\psi,S_-(f)\psi\in F_0$; $S_+(f)$ is linear in $f$ and
$S_-(f)$ is conjugate-linear in $f$; and with
$\|\psi\|_1^2:=\sum_{n}\bigl(n+1\bigr)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for $\psi\in F_0$,
$$\|S_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1,\qquad \|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$

(c) *Adjoint relation.* $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S_-(f)\psi\rangle$
for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$
([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$,
$$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$
and consequently
$$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$

Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no
physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\text{ for every }n,\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]], [[def-separable-space]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: [Contraction estimate] Let $\Psi\in D(H_f)$ and $n\ge0$; represent $\Psi_{n+1}\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)}$ by its symmetric function $F$ under [F3]. For $v\in\mathbb C^3$ define the first-factor contraction $C_v:(\mathbb C^3)^{\otimes(n+1)}\to(\mathbb C^3)^{\otimes n}$ by $C_v(a\otimes b)=\langle a,v\rangle b$, extended linearly; finite orthonormal coordinates give $\|C_v\|\le\|v\|$. The contraction is represented by the tensor-valued function $G(k')=\int C_{g(k_1)}F(k_1,k')\,dk_1$: unweighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives integrable slices almost everywhere, Fubini identifies the pairing first for elementary tensors and then by density, and the bounded contraction formula [F1] extends the identity. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz, tested against unit vectors of the finite-dimensional target tensor space, gives $\|G(k')\|^2\le\bigl(\int\|g(k_1)\|^2/\varepsilon(k_1)\,dk_1\bigr)\bigl(\int\varepsilon(k_1)\|F(k_1,k')\|^2\,dk_1\bigr)$; the null point $k_1=0$ is omitted. Integrating over $k'$ and using the symmetry computation of [F3] gives $\|\Psi_g^{(n)}\Psi_{n+1}\|^2\le\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2\cdot\frac1{n+1}\langle\varepsilon_{n+1}F,F\rangle=\frac1{n+1}\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2\langle\varepsilon_{n+1}\Psi_{n+1},\Psi_{n+1}\rangle$. Hence $\|(A_-(g)\Psi)_n\|^2=(n+1)\|\Psi_g^{(n)}\Psi_{n+1}\|^2\le\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2\langle\varepsilon_{n+1}\Psi_{n+1},\Psi_{n+1}\rangle$; summing over $n$ and using [F2] gives $\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2\le\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle$.

[The free part] Let $H_a=\sum_{a=1}^{d'}E_aP_a$ be the spectral decomposition of the Hermitian matrix $H_a$ ($d'\le d$, $P_a$ the spectral projections). Then $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)=\bigoplus_a(P_a\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h))$ and $H_0$ acts as $E_a+H_f$ on the $a$-th summand with domain $P_a\mathbb C^d\otimes D(H_f)$; by the finite direct-sum argument of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (c) (componentwise closedness and the componentwise adjoint test), $H_0$ is self-adjoint on $C^d\otimes D(H_f)$.

[The norm identity on $D(H_f)$] Let $\Psi\in D(H_f)$ and let $\Psi^{(N)}$ be its truncations to sectors $\le N$. Step 1.1 gives $A_-(g)\Psi^{(N)}\to A_-(g)\Psi$ and $\Psi^{(N)}\to\Psi$. For $N>M$, $\chi:=\Psi^{(N)}-\Psi^{(M)}$ is in $F_0$, so [F5] gives $\|A_+(g)\chi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\chi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\chi\|^2\to0$ as $M,N\to\infty$. Thus $A_+(g)\Psi^{(N)}$ is Cauchy; closedness of $A_+(g)$ from [F1] implies $\Psi\in D(A_+(g))$ and $A_+(g)\Psi^{(N)}\to A_+(g)\Psi$. Passing to the limit in [F5] for $\Psi^{(N)}$ now proves $\|A_+(g)\Psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\Psi\|^2$.

[The relative bound] From steps 1.1 and 2.1, $\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\|A_-(g)\Psi\|+\|A_+(g)\Psi\|\le2\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|\sqrt{\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle}+\|g\|\|\Psi\|$ for $\Psi\in D(H_f)$; since $\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle\le\|H_f\Psi\|\,\|\Psi\|$ by [F4], the inequality $2\sqrt{ab}\le\eta a+\eta^{-1}b$ with $a=\|H_f\Psi\|$, $b=\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2\|\Psi\|$ gives, for every $\eta>0$, $\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\|$ with $C_\eta=\eta^{-1}\|g/\sqrt\varepsilon\|^2+\|g\|$. This proves (a) and shows the $H_f$-bound zero.

[Symmetry of $\phi(g)$] For $\Psi,\Phi\in D(H_f)$, steps 1.1-1.2 show that both sides below converge absolutely, and the mutual adjointness $A_+(g)=A_-(g)^*$ of [F1] gives $\langle\phi(g)\Psi,\Phi\rangle=\langle A_-(g)\Psi,\Phi\rangle+\langle A_+(g)\Psi,\Phi\rangle=\langle\Psi,A_+(g)\Phi\rangle+\langle\Psi,A_-(g)\Phi\rangle=\langle\Psi,\phi(g)\Phi\rangle$. By step 3.1, $\phi(g)$ is symmetric on the dense domain $D(H_f)$ with $H_f$-bound zero, which is (b).

[Kato-Rellich] Let $B:=\eta_0\sum_jD_j\otimes\phi(g_j)$ with domain $C^d\otimes D(H_f)$. Since the $D_j$ are bounded and each $\phi(g_j)$ is symmetric with $H_f$-bound zero (step 4.1, step 3.1), $B$ is symmetric and for every $\eta>0$ there are finite constants with $\|B\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\|$; as $H_0$ differs from $I\otimes H_f$ by the bounded operator $H_a\otimes I$, the same estimate holds with $H_f$ replaced by $H_0$ up to constants, so the $H_0$-bound of $B$ is zero and in particular less than $1$. As $H_0$ is self-adjoint (step 1.2), [F6] gives that $H=H_0+B$ is self-adjoint on $C^d\otimes D(H_f)$ and bounded below. This proves (c).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a), step 4.1 proves (b), and steps 1.2 and 5.1 prove (c). The final paragraph of the statement records that the normalisation of the coupling and of the dipole matrices is a model choice, and no physical radiation or emission statement is asserted. This completes the proof.
