Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

For every double sequence $(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb N}$ in $[0,+\infty]$,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right)=\sup_{m,n\in\mathbb N}\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{ij}\right),$$

where every sum is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]]. Thus the order of summation may be interchanged, even when the common value is $+\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals ([[def-sequence]]) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing ([[def-monotone-sequence]]) and $S$ is bounded
   above ([[def-bounded-set]]), then $(x_k)$ converges ([[def-real-limit]]) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) supplies the
first and [[thm-infimum-property]] the second, and each is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

derivations.claim: [Single orbital] The vector $u_k$ is an eigenvector of $\sum_{m=0}^1mT_{u_m,u_m}$ with eigenvalue $k$, so $e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)N_-}=\sum_{k=0}^1e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)k}T_{u_k,u_k}=F$ on a complete orthonormal family, hence everywhere; $F$ is a positive diagonal finite-rank operator with eigenvalues $1$ and $e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}>0$. By [F2] its trace is $1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}$ and the weighted average of the eigenvalues $0,1$ is $\frac{0\cdot1+1\cdot e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}}{1+e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}}=\frac1{e^{\beta(\varepsilon_1-\mu)}+1}$. This proves (a).

[Dilute remainders] For $0<q<1$, the algebra $\frac{q}{1-q}-q=\frac{q^2}{1-q}$ and $\frac q{1+q}-q=-\frac{q^2}{1+q}$ is immediate; both error terms are positive and bounded by $2q^2$ when $q\le1/2$ because $1-q\ge1/2$ and $1+q\ge1/2$. The displayed geometric sums are [F1]. This proves (c).

[Fermionic products] If infinitely many $j$ have $q_j>1/2$, the product over any $k$ of these indices is at least $(3/2)^k$, so $Z_{\mathrm F}=+\infty$ and $\sum_jq_j=+\infty$. Otherwise their finitely many factors are finite positive constants, and [F3] gives $q_j/2\le q_j-q_j^2\le\log(1+q_j)\le q_j$ on the remaining tail. Thus the nonnegative logarithmic partial sums are bounded exactly when $\sum_jq_j<\infty$. Since $\prod_{j\le n}(1+q_j)=\exp(\sum_{j\le n}\log(1+q_j))$, the increasing partial products have a finite limit exactly in that case. Every finite subset is contained in an initial segment and every factor is at least one, so their supremum equals that limit. Finally $\sum_jq_j=e^{\beta\mu}\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}$, giving precisely the fermionic equivalence in (b).

[Bosonic products] If some $\varepsilon_j\le\mu$, then $q_j\ge1$ and $Z_{\mathrm B}=+\infty$ by the stated convention; also $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j$ fails. Suppose all $q_j<1$. By [F4], $q_j\le-\log(1-q_j)$ for every index. If infinitely many $q_j>1/2$, both corresponding sums diverge; otherwise discard only that finite set and use $q_j\le-\log(1-q_j)\le2q_j$ on its complement. Consequently $\sum_j-\log(1-q_j)<\infty$ exactly when $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, and the reciprocal partial products, whose logarithms are these partial sums, have a finite limit exactly then. Their limit equals the finite-subset supremum because the factors are at least one. If $\sum_jq_j<\infty$, then $q_j\to0$, so $\varepsilon_j\to+\infty$ since $q_j=e^{-\beta(\varepsilon_j-\mu)}$ and $\beta>0$. In particular, all but finitely many $\varepsilon_j$ exceed $\varepsilon_1$; hence the infimum is attained in a nonempty finite initial set. Since every $\varepsilon_j>\mu$, this gives $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j$. Conversely, $\mu<\inf_j\varepsilon_j$ and $\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$ imply all $q_j<1$ and $\sum_jq_j=e^{\beta\mu}\sum_je^{-\beta\varepsilon_j}<\infty$, so the scalar criterion just proved gives finite $Z_{\mathrm B}$. This proves the full bosonic equivalence without assuming attainment in the hypotheses and without invoking an Axiom-of-Choice spectral theorem.

[Conclusion] Steps 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and 1.4 establish (a), (c), the fermionic half of (b) and the bosonic half of (b) respectively; in the finite cases the displayed products are the limits, and the mode occupancies in (c) are the normalized geometric sums of [F1]. The closing paragraph of the statement records that no physical identification of the parameters or of the products with thermodynamic quantities is asserted.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: [The Gibbs state and its entropy] The weights $q_j:=e^{-\beta E_j}/Z$ are positive with $\sum_jq_j=1$, so by [F1] and [F2] $\rho_\beta=\sum_jq_jT_{v_j,v_j}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator with orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_j)$, eigenvalues $q_j$ and trace $1$; hence $\rho_\beta\in\mathcal D$. Its entropy is $s(\rho_\beta)=-\sum_jq_j\log q_j=\sum_jq_j(\beta E_j+\log Z)=\beta\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)+\log Z$ by [F2], where $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\sum_jq_jE_j$. Rearranging gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, which is (a).

[The doubly stochastic matrix] Let $p_{ij}:=|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2$. Since $(u_i)$ and $(v_j)$ are orthonormal bases, [F1] gives $p_{ij}\ge0$, $\sum_jp_{ij}=\|u_i\|^2=1$ and $\sum_ip_{ij}=\|v_j\|^2=1$: the matrix $(p_{ij})$ is doubly stochastic. For $r_i:=\sum_jp_{ij}q_j$ one has $r_i>0$ because all $q_j>0$ and $\sum_jp_{ij}=1$, and $\sum_ir_i=\sum_jq_j\sum_ip_{ij}=1$.

[The entropy bound and equality case] For $x>1$, the integral formula in [F3] gives $\log x=\int_1^x dt/t<x-1$, because $1/t<1$ for $t>1$; for $0<x<1$, put $y=1/x>1$. On $[1,y)$ one has $1/t>1/y=x$, so $\log y=\int_1^y dt/t> x(y-1)=1-x$, and the reciprocal law gives $\log x=-\log y<x-1$. Thus $\log x\le x-1$ for every $x>0$, with equality exactly at $x=1$. Let $S:=\{i:w_i>0\}$ and $k:=|S|$, so $1\le k\le d$. Then
Since $0<w_i\le1$, every term $-w_i\log w_i=w_i\log(1/w_i)$ is nonnegative. Also
$$s(\rho)-\log d=\sum_{i\in S}w_i\log\frac1{dw_i}\le\sum_{i\in S}w_i\left(\frac1{dw_i}-1\right)=\frac{k}{d}-1\le0.$$
If $s(\rho)=\log d$, then $k=d$ and equality holds in every positive-weight logarithm inequality, since each individual difference $w_i[(1/(dw_i)-1)-\log(1/(dw_i))]$ is nonnegative and their finite sum is zero. The equality characterization above forces $1/(dw_i)=1$ for all $i$, so $w_i=1/d$ and $\rho=\sum_i(1/d)T_{u_i,u_i}=d^{-1}\mathrm{id}$. Conversely $\rho=d^{-1}\mathrm{id}$ has entropy $\log d$. When $H=0$ all $E_j=0$, so $Z=d$ and $\rho_\beta=d^{-1}\mathrm{id}$, and the bound of (b) is attained there.

[Relative entropy is nonnegative] With $w_i$ the eigenvalues of $\rho$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis $(u_i)$ of [F1], $\log\rho=\sum_{i:w_i>0}(\log w_i)T_{u_i,u_i}$ and $\log\rho_\beta=\sum_j(\log q_j)T_{v_j,v_j}$ (finite-dimensional spectral calculus). For the product with $\rho$, the symbol $\log\rho$ here denotes the logarithm on the positive spectral support extended by zero on $\ker\rho$; it does not assign a value to $\log0$. Thus by [F2] $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)=\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\log w_i$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho_\beta)=\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\sum_jp_{ij}\log q_j$. For each $i$ with $w_i>0$, $r_i=\sum_jp_{ij}q_j>0$ and $\sum_jp_{ij}=1$ by step 1.2. Applying $\log x\le x-1$ from step 1.3 to $x=q_j/r_i$ and summing with weights $p_{ij}$ gives $\sum_jp_{ij}\log(q_j/r_i)\le\sum_jp_{ij}(q_j/r_i-1)=0$, hence $\sum_jp_{ij}\log q_j\le\log r_i$. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho_\beta)\ge\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i(\log w_i-\log r_i)=\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\log(w_i/r_i)$. Writing $w_i\log(w_i/r_i)=-w_i\log(r_i/w_i)$ and again applying step 1.3 to $x=r_i/w_i>0$ gives $w_i\log(w_i/r_i)\ge w_i-r_i$; summing, $\sum_{i:w_i>0}(w_i-r_i)=1-\sum_{i:w_i>0}r_i=\sum_{i:w_i=0}r_i\ge0$, since $\sum_ir_i=1$ by step 1.2. Therefore $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)\ge\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho_\beta)$.

[The lower bound] By the spectral description of $\rho_\beta$ in step 1.1, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho_\beta)=\sum_j(\log q_j)\operatorname{tr}(\rho T_{v_j,v_j})=\sum_j(-\beta E_j-\log Z)\langle\rho v_j,v_j\rangle=-\beta\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\log Z$, since $\sum_j\langle\rho v_j,v_j\rangle=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)=\sum_jE_j\langle\rho v_j,v_j\rangle$ (because $H=\sum_jE_jT_{v_j,v_j}$). Combining with step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)\ge-\beta\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\log Z$; multiplying by $\beta^{-1}$ and rearranging, using $s(\rho)=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\log\rho)$, gives the bound (b).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1-3.1 prove (a), (b) and (c), including the asserted equality in (a) and the attainment in (c). The final paragraph of the statement records that the thermodynamic reading of the functional and of $\rho_\beta$ requires additional physical assumptions, which are not part of this mathematical statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
including $n=0$, a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given (so $T_0$ is a
self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb C$),
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

derivations.claim: [Oscillator coefficients] For $e_m$ supported in coordinate $m$, the raising formula of [F3] has its only nonzero coordinate at $m+1$, with value $\sqrt{m+1}$, so $A_+(1)e_m=\sqrt{m+1}e_{m+1}$. For $m\ge1$ the lowering formula has its only nonzero coordinate at $m-1$, with value $\sqrt m$, so $A_-(1)e_m=\sqrt m\,e_{m-1}$; for $m=0$ every lowering coordinate is zero. This proves (a).

[Convergence and normalization] Let $z\in\mathbb C$ and $S_N:=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{n\le N}z^n/\sqrt{n!}\,e_n$. Orthogonality of the $e_n$ gives $\|S_N-S_M\|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\sum_{M<n\le N}|z|^{2n}/n!$, and $\sum_n|z|^{2n}/n!=\exp(|z|^2)$ by [F4], so $(S_N)$ is Cauchy and converges in the complete space $F(\mathbb C)$ to a vector $\psi_z$; moreover $\|\psi_z\|^2=\lim_N\|S_N\|^2=e^{-|z|^2}\exp(|z|^2)=1$, so $\|\psi_z\|=1$. For $z=0$ only the zeroth term survives, so convergence is absolute. For $z\ne0$, convergence is absolute because the ratio of consecutive moduli of $\sum_n|z|^n/\sqrt{n!}$ is $|z|/\sqrt{n+1}\to0$, so that series converges by the ratio test ([[thm-ratio-test]]); and $\sum_n|z|^{2n}/n!=\exp(|z|^2)$ is the exponential series of the real number $|z|^2\ge0$ ([F4]).

[Annihilation eigenvalue] Every finite combination $S_N\in F_0$ lies in the domain of the closed operator $A_-(1)$, and $A_-(1)S_N=e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{1\le n\le N}z^n/\sqrt{n!}\sqrt n\,e_{n-1}=z\,e^{-|z|^2/2}\sum_{0\le m\le N-1}z^m/\sqrt{m!}\,e_m\to z\psi_z$ by step 1.2. Since $S_N\to\psi_z$ and $A_-(1)$ is closed, $\psi_z\in D(A_-(1))$ and $A_-(1)\psi_z=z\psi_z$.

[Overlaps and the number law] For $z,w\in\mathbb C$, the series $\psi_z$ and $\psi_w$ have absolutely convergent coordinate expansions, so the inner product may be computed termwise: $\langle\psi_z,\psi_w\rangle=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2}\sum_n z^n\overline{w^n}/n!=e^{-(|z|^2+|w|^2)/2+z\overline w}$, the last equality by the exponential series [F4] and its addition law [F5]. In particular $\|\psi_z\|^2=\langle\psi_z,\psi_z\rangle=e^{-|z|^2+|z|^2}=1$. Since $|\langle e_n,\psi_z\rangle|^2=\bigl|e^{-|z|^2/2}\overline{z}^n/\sqrt{n!}\bigr|^2=e^{-|z|^2}|z|^{2n}/n!$ and $\sum_n|z|^{2n}/n!=\exp(|z|^2)$, the weights in (c) sum to $1$.

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1-2.2 prove (a), (b) and (c); the square roots $\sqrt{n!}$ and $\sqrt{n}$ are the positive real roots. The final statement records that no measurement postulate, and hence no probability interpretation of the displayed weights, is asserted; the Fock vectors and the eigenvalue relation are purely mathematical.

risk_review.notes: Checked Proof 1.1–5.1 against the three-dimensional Hardy, Sobolev density, a.e. subsequence, Fatou, Tonelli and Kato–Rellich suppliers. Slice Hardy handles each center; the orthogonal pair coordinate gives the factor 2 bound. Kinetic-gradient identities use the correct 8pi² normalization; Young inequality yields operator bound zero, separately from the form bound. Finite coefficient sums remain infinitesimally K-bounded; a<1 gives equivalent graph norms and the smooth core. Equal masses and symmetric Coulomb coefficients satisfy permutation reduction (d), unaffected by the F4 repair. Empty center/pair sums, zero coefficients, coincident centers and singular null sets do not invalidate the domain estimates. Accepted reader L2 Cauchy–Schwarz citation correction.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $N\ge1$, let
$m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and $\hbar>0$, write points of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ as
$X=(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ with $x_i\in\mathbb R^3$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the
Plancherel transform of [[thm-plancherel]] with the convention
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(X)e^{-2\pi iX\cdot\xi}\,dX$ on $L^1$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]]). Define the quadratic weight and the
free kinetic operator
$$\kappa(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_N):=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_i}|\xi_i|^2,\qquad K:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_\kappa\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(K):=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C):\ \kappa\,\mathcal F_2u\in L^2\}$$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]).
Let $V:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and bounded, with
$\|V\|_\infty:=\operatorname{ess\,sup}|V|<\infty$, and let $M_V$ be
multiplication by $V$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]],
[[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

(a) $K$ is a self-adjoint positive operator with domain $D(K)$, and $D(K)$ is
the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$ as a set, with
$\|\cdot\|_{W^{2,2}}$ equivalent to the graph norm
$u\mapsto(\|u\|^2+\|Ku\|^2)^{1/2}$
([[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]],
[[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]]);

(b) $H:=K+M_V$ with $D(H):=D(K)$ is self-adjoint and bounded below by
$-\|V\|_\infty$; the space $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)$ is a core for
both $K$ and $H$ ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[cor-compactly-supported-smooth-functions-are-dense-in-wkp-of-rn]],
[[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]);

(c) for every $r\ge1$ the operator $K\otimes I_r+M_V\otimes I_r$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)\otimes\mathbb C^r$, with domain
$D(K)\otimes\mathbb C^r$, is self-adjoint and bounded below by $-\|V\|_\infty$.

In particular, if $V_i:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ and $W_{ij}:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$
($1\le i<j\le N$) are measurable and bounded and
$V(X):=\sum_iV_i(x_i)+\sum_{i<j}W_{ij}(x_i-x_j)$, then $\|V\|_\infty\le\sum_i\|V_i\|_\infty+\sum_{i<j}\|W_{ij}\|_\infty<\infty$
and (a)-(c) apply. No Hunziker-van Winter-Zhislin threshold statement, no
stability of matter, no thermodynamic-limit and no physical interpretation is
asserted.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] with the weak gradient $\nabla u$ of
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]], write
$r(x):=|x|$, and write $\|u\|_2^2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u(x)|^2\,dx$ for the
$L^2$ norm of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Then:

(a) for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\};\mathbb C)$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{|u(x)|^2}{|x|^2}\,dx\le 4\int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla u(x)|^2\,dx;$$

(b) the same inequality holds for every $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$;

(c) for every $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ the a.e.-defined function $x\mapsto u(x)/|x|$ lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and satisfies $\|u/|\cdot|\|_2\le 2\|\nabla u\|_2$.

No constant smaller than $4$ is claimed, and no statement is made about
$\|u/|\cdot|\|_2$ for $u$ outside $W^{1,2}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Assume countable choice. For every measure space and $1\le p\le\infty$, $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is complete. Every sequence converging in this norm has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to a measurable representative of its norm limit. For finite $p$ no pointwise convergence of the whole sequence is asserted.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $T$ be an orthogonal operator on
$\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean inner product
([[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for every
Lebesgue measurable $E$ and

$$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; \lambda_n(E).$$

Both the orientation-preserving operators, of determinant $1$, and those of
determinant $-1$ are covered, since only the absolute value of the determinant
enters; nothing is asserted here about which matrices occur in either class.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Work on a complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first variable. Let $A$ be self-adjoint and let $B$ be symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and
$A$-bound less than one ([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]]).
Then $A+B$ with domain $D(A)$ is self-adjoint. If $A$ is merely essentially
self-adjoint and $B$ is symmetric with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and $A$-bound less
than one, then $A+B$ on $D(A)$ is essentially self-adjoint and its closure is
the self-adjoint operator obtained by applying the first part to $\overline A$
and the graph-norm extension of $B|_{D(A)}$ to $D(\overline A)$. If $A\ge\gamma$ and
$(a,b)$ is an admissible pair for $B$ with $a<1$, then
$A+B\ge\gamma-\max\{a|\gamma|+b,\ b/(1-a)\}$.

Let $A$ be a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(A)$. An operator $B$ is
**$A$-bounded**, or **relatively bounded with respect to $A$**, when
$D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ and there are finite constants $a,b\ge0$ with
$$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|\qquad\text{for all }x\in D(A).$$
The infimum of the admissible constants $a$ is the **$A$-bound** of $B$, and
one says the $A$-bound is *below one* when some $a<1$ is admissible.

**Equivalent form.** $B$ is $A$-bounded exactly when $B$ is bounded on $D(A)$
for the graph norm $\|x\|_A=(\|x\|^2+\|Ax\|^2)^{1/2}$ of
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]: each estimate
$\|Bx\|\le a\|Ax\|+b\|x\|$ gives
$\|Bx\|\le\max(a,b)\sqrt2\,\|x\|_A$, and conversely a graph-norm bound
$\|Bx\|\le C\|x\|_A$ gives the estimate with $a=b=C$. The constant $b$ is not
intrinsic, and no closedness, density or resolvent hypothesis is needed for
the definition. If $A$ is closed with nonempty resolvent set, then $A$-bounded
operators are exactly those with $D(A)\subseteq D(B)$ for which $BR_A(z)$ is
bounded for some, equivalently every, $z\in\rho(A)$
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]]). Indeed, an
$A$-bound makes $BR_A(z)$ bounded because
$AR_A(z)=zR_A(z)-I$; conversely, if $BR_A(z)$ is bounded, then
$Bx=BR_A(z)(z-A)x$ gives an $A$-bound. Thus boundedness for one resolvent
implies relative boundedness and hence boundedness for every resolvent. This
is used in the Kato-Rellich theorem below and recorded here as an interface.

derivations.claim:
[Global Hardy inequalities] Let $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{3N})$ and fix a block index $i$ and a center $a\in\mathbb R^3$. For each fixed value of the remaining coordinates the slice $x_i\mapsto u(\dots,x_i,\dots)$ is a compactly supported smooth function on $\mathbb R^3$; [F2] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|u|^2/|x_i-a|^2\,dx_i\le4\int_{\mathbb R^3}|
abla_iu|^2dx_i$ for that slice, and integrating over the remaining coordinates by Tonelli [F3] with [F4] (translation to the center $a$) yields $\int|u|^2/|x_i-a|^2\le4\int|
abla_iu|^2$. For a pair replace $(x_i,x_j)$ by the orthogonal coordinates $(y,z)$ of [F4]: then $|x_i-x_j|^2=2|y|^2$ and, applying the same slice argument in the $y$-variable to the transformed function, $\int|u|^2/|x_i-x_j|^2=	frac12\int|u'|^2/|y|^2\le2\int|
abla_yu'|^2\le2\int(|
abla_iu|^2+|
abla_ju|^2)$. Both inequalities extend to all $u\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{3N})$: choose $u_k\in C_c^\infty$ with $u_k	o u$ and $
abla u_k	o
abla u$ in $L^2$ ([F3]); the right-hand sides converge to the corresponding norms of $u$, while the left-hand sides are lower semicontinuous by Fatou along an a.e. convergent subsequence ([F3]).

[Operator-norm $K$-bounds] Let $u\in D(K)$ and put $a:=\|Ku\|_2$, $b:=\|u\|_2$. The squared Hardy bound of step 1.1 and [F1] give $\|u/|x_i-a_m|\|_2^2\le4\|
abla_iu\|_2^2\le(32\pi^2m_i/\hbar^2)\langle Ku,uangle\le(32\pi^2m_i/\hbar^2)ab$. For a pair, the corrected pair bound gives $\|u/|x_i-x_j|\|_2^2\le2(\|
abla_iu\|_2^2+\|
abla_ju\|_2^2)\le(16\pi^2\max(m_i,m_j)/\hbar^2)\langle Ku,uangle\le(16\pi^2\max(m_i,m_j)/\hbar^2)ab$: the sum uses $\langle(K_i+K_j)u,uangle\le\langle Ku,uangle$. For either multiplier let $C$ be the square root of its displayed finite coefficient. For every $\eta>0$, $C\sqrt{ab}\le\eta a+C^2b/(4\eta)$, obtained by expanding $(\sqrt{\eta a}-C\sqrt{b}/(2\sqrt\eta))^2\ge0$. Thus both actual $L^2$ operator norms are at most $\eta\|Ku\|_2+C_\eta\|u\|_2$, with finite $C_\eta=C^2/(4\eta)$, including $u=0$. No form-to-operator-norm inference is used. This proves (a) for the literal Fourier-normalized $K$ of the supplier.

[Separate quadratic-form bound] The same norm Hardy and kinetic-gradient inequalities give $\|u/r\|_2\le C\langle Ku,u\rangle^{1/2}$ for each distance multiplier, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\langle M_Vu,u\rangle|\le\int|V||u|^2\le C_V\langle Ku,u\rangle^{1/2}\|u\|_2$, where $C_V$ is the finite sum of the respective Hardy-gradient constants times $|z_{im}|,|z_{ij}|$. For every $\epsilon>0$, Young's square inequality yields $|\langle M_Vu,u\rangle|\le\epsilon\langle Ku,u\rangle+C_V^2\|u\|_2^2/(4\epsilon)$. In particular $\langle(K+M_V)u,u\rangle\ge(1-\epsilon)\langle Ku,u\rangle-C_V^2\|u\|_2^2/(4\epsilon)$; this is a valid form bound and lower estimate, separate from the operator-norm bound of step 2.1.

[The full multiplier and Kato-Rellich] Since $V$ is a finite real linear combination of the multipliers of part (a), each with $K$-bound zero, $V$ is measurable and $M_V$ is a symmetric operator with $D(K)\subseteq D(M_V)$ and $K$-bound zero ([F5]); in particular the bound $\|M_Vu\|\le a\|Ku\|+b\|u\|$ holds on $D(K)$ for some $a<1$ and finite $b$ (choose $a<1$ by the zero bound and adjust $b$). By [F5] (Kato-Rellich) $H=K+M_V$ is self-adjoint on $D(K)$ and bounded below. Since the graph norms of $H$ and $K$ are equivalent on $D(K)$ (as in [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (b)), the core $C_c^\infty$ of $K$ is a core for $H$. This proves (b).

[Component extension and permutation sectors] The passage to $L^2(\mathbb R^{3N};\mathbb C)\otimes\mathbb C^r$ is the finite direct sum of $r$ copies of $H$ and is self-adjoint and bounded below by the same argument as part (c) of [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]]; this proves (c). Under equal masses and permutation-invariant coefficients, both $K$ and the multiplier $M_V$ are invariant under the transported permutation unitaries (the weight $\kappa$ and the multiplier $V$ are permutation invariant, and the domain $D(M_V)$ is permutation invariant because the a.e.-defined function $V$ is), so $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}D(H)=D(H)$ and $U_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}H=HU_\pi^{\mathrm{phys}}$ on $D(H)$; part (d) then follows from [[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-permutation-restricted-self-adjointness]] (d).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1 prove (a)-(d). The final paragraph of the statement records the excluded claims: no HVZ threshold, no uniform-in-$N$ stability, no thermodynamic limit, no further spectral statement and no physical interpretation is asserted.
