Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Let
$H^{\otimes 0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes 1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(n+1)}:=H^{\otimes n}\widehat\otimes H$ be the completed tensor
powers with elementary tensors $u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_n$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]); for $n\ge 1$ let
$P_+^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ be the symmetric projection of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]] and set
$P_+^{(0)}:=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$. Write $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ for
its range and define

$$F(H):=\Bigl\{\psi=(\psi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}:\ \psi_n\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$

Then:

(a) for $\psi,\varphi\in F(H)$ the scalar series
$\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$ converges absolutely and
defines a sesquilinear form, linear in the first argument, with respect to
which $F(H)$ is a complex vector space with inner product
$\langle\psi,\varphi\rangle:=\sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\langle\psi_n,\varphi_n\rangle$
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]]);

(b) $(F(H),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. the induced norm
is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]);

(c) the vacuum vector $\Omega:=(1,0,0,\dots)$ satisfies $\|\Omega\|=1$, and the
finite-particle space
$F_0:=\{\psi\in F(H):\psi_n=0\ \text{for all but finitely many }n\}$ is a dense
linear subspace of $F(H)$ ([[def-dense-top]]);

(d) for every $n$ the map
$\iota_n:\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\to F(H)$,
$\iota_n(u):=(0,\dots,0,u,0,\dots)$ (entry in coordinate $n$) is a linear
isometry of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ onto the closed subspace of vectors
supported in coordinate $n$;

(e) if $H$ admits a countable complete orthonormal family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$, $I$ at most countable
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]),
then $F(H)$ is separable ([[def-separable-space]]);

(f) *direct sums of self-adjoint operators*: if for every $n\in\mathbb N$,
including $n=0$, a self-adjoint operator $T_n$ on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with domain
$D(T_n)\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is given (so $T_0$ is a
self-adjoint operator on $\mathbb C$),
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-unbounded-linear-operator-domain-and-graph]]), and

$$D(T):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\ \text{for all }n,\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (T\psi)_n:=T_n\psi_n,$$

then $T$ is self-adjoint and $D(T)$ is dense; if in addition every $T_n$ is
bounded with $\sup_{n}\|T_n\|<\infty$, then $T$ is bounded with
$\|T\|=\sup_n\|T_n\|$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

No physical interpretation of $F(H)$, of the tensor powers or of the direct-sum
operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $E$ be a projection valued measure on the
measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on the complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be
$\Sigma$-measurable. Put
$$D(f(E)):=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_X|f|^2\,dE_x<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,$$
where the scalar measures $E_x$ are those of
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]], and for $x\in D(f(E))$ set
$$f(E)x:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi_E\bigl(f\,\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}\bigr)x,$$
For $H\ne\{0\}$, the bounded integrals $\Phi_E$ are those of
[[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], and the limit is taken in the norm of $H$.
For $H=\{0\}$, define $\Phi_E(g)$ to be the unique operator on $H$ for every bounded measurable $g$. Then $E_0$ is the zero measure, $D(f(E))=H$, and $f(E)0=0$. Thus this case is defined directly without applying a theorem requiring a nonzero space.

**Well-definedness.** $D(f(E))$ is a linear subspace: the estimate
$E_{x+y}\le2E_x+2E_y$ for scalar measures and $E_{\alpha x}=|\alpha|^2E_x$
follow from $\|E(B)(x+y)\|^2\le2\|E(B)x\|^2+2\|E(B)y\|^2$ and
$\|E(B)\alpha x\|^2=|\alpha|^2\|E(B)x\|^2$. Writing $f_n:=f\mathbf 1_{\{|f|\le n\}}$
the sets $\{|f|\le n\}$ are measurable, so $f_n$ is bounded and measurable.
For $m,n\ge N$,
$$|f_n-f_m|^2\le |f|^2\mathbf1_{\{|f|>N\}}.$$
The integral of the right side against $E_x$ tends to zero by
[[thm-dominated-convergence]], with the integrable majorant $|f|^2$ and
pointwise limit zero since $f$ is finite-valued. Linearity of the bounded
calculus ([[thm-pvm-integral-is-a-star-homomorphism]]) and its quadratic identity give
$$\|\Phi_E(f_n)x-\Phi_E(f_m)x\|^2=\int|f_n-f_m|^2\,dE_x.$$
These clauses hold directly on the zero space as well. Hence the truncation
vectors are Cauchy and converge uniquely by Hilbert-space completeness
([[def-hilbert-space]]). The limit is linear in $x$ because every truncation
operator is linear and addition and scalar multiplication are norm-continuous.
Countable Choice is inherited from the bounded PVM suppliers; no further
choice is needed to take these specified limits.

Finally, if two $\Sigma$-measurable functions $f,g$ agree outside a measurable
set $N$ with $E(N)=0$, then $E_x(N)=\|E(N)x\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Thus the
integrals of $|f|^2$ and $|g|^2$ agree, so their domains agree. At every
truncation level their bounded truncations agree outside $N$; the quadratic
identity applied to the difference gives equal truncation vectors for every
$x$. Taking limits gives $f(E)x=g(E)x$ on their common domain.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space with $\mu(X)>0$, let $m:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and finite $\mu$-almost everywhere, and on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^{2}(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) let
$$D(M_{m})=\Bigl\{f\in H:\int_{X}|m|^{2}|f|^{2}\,d\mu<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad M_{m}f=mf .$$
Then:

(a) $M_m$ is self-adjoint on $D(M_m)$.

(b) The assignment $E(B):=M_{\mathbf 1_{m^{-1}(B)}}$ on Borel sets $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular projection-valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and for a unit vector $\psi\in H$
$$\|E(B)\psi\|^{2}=\int_{m^{-1}(B)}|\psi|^{2}\,d\mu .$$

(c) The operator identity $\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)=M_{m}$ holds with domain $D(M_{m})$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); consequently $E$ is the spectral projection-valued measure of $M_{m}$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]).

(d) $E(B)=0$ if and only if $\mu(m^{-1}(B))=0$, and the spectrum $\sigma(M_{m})$ equals the essential range of $m$:
$$\sigma(M_{m})=\{\,t\in\mathbb R:\mu(m^{-1}(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon))>0\ \text{for every}\ \varepsilon>0\,\}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $X$ and $Y$
be normed spaces over the same scalar field
([[def-norm-and-normed-space]], [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]])
and let $T:X\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Then $T$ is compact
([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) if and only if every bounded sequence
$(x_k)$ in $X$, that is every function $x:\mathbb N\to X$ with bounded range
([[def-sequence]], [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]), has a subsequence
$(x_{k_j})$, the index map being strictly increasing
([[def-metric-compactness-variants]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]), for which
$(Tx_{k_j})$ converges in the norm metric of $Y$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

If $K\subseteq U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $K$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq U$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable ([[def-countable]]) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Recall that a natural number is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$ and $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, so
that

$$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\} = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$$

is itself the set of its predecessors. Here $<$ is the order of
[[def-nat-order]], which is defined additively, so the displayed identity is a
theorem and not a convention: it is [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], proved
immediately above. Let $A$ be a set, and let $\approx$ be equinumerosity
([[def-equinumerous]]).

- $A$ is **finite** if $A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **countably infinite** if $A \approx \mathbb{N}$.
- $A$ is **at most countable** if it is finite or countably infinite.
- $A$ is **uncountable** if it is not at most countable.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

derivations.claim:
[Finite components and reducing restrictions] The scalar self-adjointness in [F2] extends to any finite number of components: the multiplication domain is the finite product of scalar domains, hence dense, and testing the adjoint identity with a vector supported in one component shows that the adjoint domain and action are exactly the componentwise multiplication domain and action. Now let $A$ be self-adjoint, let $Q$ be a bounded orthogonal projection with $QD(A)\subseteq D(A)$ and $AQx=QAx$ on $D(A)$, and put $K=\operatorname{ran}Q$. The domain $D(A)\cap K$ is dense in $K$, since applying $Q$ to approximants in the dense $D(A)$ gives approximants in this intersection. The restriction $A_K$ is symmetric. If $y\in D(A_K^*)$ and $h=A_K^*y\in K$, then for every $x\in D(A)$, [F2, algebra]
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle QAx,y\rangle=\langle AQx,y\rangle=\langle Qx,h\rangle=\langle x,h\rangle.$$
Thus $y\in D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $Ay=h$, so $y\in D(A_K)$ and $A_K^*y=A_Ky$. Conversely symmetry gives $A_K\subseteq A_K^*$. Therefore $A_K$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(A)\cap K$. This argument uses the adjoint definition, not a missing clause of the scalar multiplier theorem.

[The transverse space] For $k\ne0$ the matrix $\Pi(k)$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\{v:k\cdot v=0\}$: it is symmetric, $\Pi(k)^2=\Pi(k)$ and $\Pi(k)v=v$ exactly for $k\cdot v=0$. Extending by $\Pi(0)=0$ gives a measurable, bounded, projection-valued function, so $M_\Pi$ is a bounded self-adjoint projection and $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed subspace. By [F10], the image under $M_\Pi$ of a countable dense subset of $G$ is countable and dense in its range, so $\mathfrak h$ is separable. Since $\varepsilon$ is radial, $M_\varepsilon M_\Pi=M_\Pi M_\varepsilon$, so $M_\varepsilon$ preserves $\mathfrak h$; by step 1.1 the restriction $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is self-adjoint with domain $\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$, and it is positive because $\varepsilon\ge0$. This proves (a).

[Transverse symmetric sectors and their energy domains] Fix $n\ge1$. The isometric inclusion $\mathfrak h\to G$ induces an isometric inclusion of the completed tensor powers, since the elementary inner products agree and their spans are dense. Under $\Theta_n$ of [F3], its closed range is that of multiplication by [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]
$$Q_n(k)=\Pi(k_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes\Pi(k_n).$$
Indeed this bounded orthogonal projection sends every elementary product to the product of its transverse projections, so its range is the closure of the transverse elementary span. Let $\tau_\pi$ permute the factors of $(\mathbb C^3)^{\otimes n}$ by the same convention as $U_\pi$. The ambient permutation is
$$(C_\pi f)(k_1,\ldots,k_n)=\tau_\pi f(k_{\pi(1)},\ldots,k_{\pi(n)}),$$
as follows first on elementary products and then everywhere by density. Hence $S_n=(n!)^{-1}\sum_\pi C_\pi$ is the orthogonal symmetric projection. The transverse tensor projection commutes with every permutation on elementary tensors, and hence everywhere; thus $R_n=M_{Q_n}S_n$ is an orthogonal projection whose range $K_n$ is exactly the image of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\subseteq\mathfrak h^{\otimes n}$. Denote the resulting isometry onto $K_n$ by $I_n$. Since each $\tau_\pi$ is unitary, every sector vector has $\|I_nu(k_{\pi(1)},\ldots,k_{\pi(n)})\|=\|I_nu(k_1,\ldots,k_n)\|$ almost everywhere. This is the norm symmetry used in sector energy integrals; it does not assert invariance of each polarization component without permuting its tensor factors.
The ambient finite-component multiplier $A_n=M_{\varepsilon_n}$ is self-adjoint on its maximal multiplication domain by step 1.1. Its domain is preserved by $M_{Q_n}$, since this pointwise projection is contractive and commutes with the scalar multiplier. It is preserved by every $C_\pi$, and $A_nC_\pi=C_\pi A_n$ on that domain, because $\varepsilon_n(k)=\sum_i\alpha|k_i|$ is permutation invariant. Therefore $R_n$ preserves the domain and commutes with $A_n$ there. Step 1.1 makes its restriction to $K_n$ self-adjoint on precisely $\{f\in K_n:\varepsilon_nf\in L_n\}$. Commutation implies that the product lies in $K_n$ whenever it lies in $L_n$. Transport by $I_n$ gives exactly $T_n$ and the displayed domain of the Statement. Its pairing with a domain vector is the integral of $\varepsilon_n\|I_n\psi\|^2$, which is nonnegative and finite by Cauchy-Schwarz [F9]. Thus $T_n\ge0$, proving (b). For $n=0$, $T_0=0$ on all of $\mathbb C$ is self-adjoint and positive.

[The free Fock Hamiltonian] By step 3.1 each $T_n$, including $T_0=0$, is self-adjoint on its sector, so [F4] gives that $H_f=\bigoplus_nT_n$ is self-adjoint on the displayed domain. For $\psi\in D(H_f)$, $\langle H_f\psi,\psi\rangle=\sum_n\langle T_n\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle\ge0$; the sum is absolutely convergent by [F9] and finite-sequence Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $(\|T_n\psi_n\|)_n$ and $(\|\psi_n\|)_n$. Since each $T_n$ maps $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ into itself, $H_f$ commutes with every sector projection $\Pi_n$. This proves (c).

[The direct-sum spectral PVM and the exponential] For each $n\ge0$ let $E_n$ be the regular spectral PVM of $T_n$ from [F5], with $E_0(B)=\mathbf1_B(0)I_{\mathbb C}$ because $T_0=0$, and define $E(B):=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}E_n(B)$. Each $E(B)$ is an orthogonal projection, $E(\mathbb R)=I$, and the PVM product law holds coordinatewise. Strong countable additivity follows by first restricting a vector to finitely many sectors, where it is the strong additivity of the $E_n$, and then bounding the omitted squared norm by the tail $\sum_{n>N}\|\psi_n\|^2$. Its scalar measure is $E_\psi(B)=\sum_{n\ge0}(E_n)_{\psi_n}(B)$; this finite measure given by a countable sum of sector measures is regular, since one first discards a tail of total mass $\sum_{n>N}\|\psi_n\|^2$ and then uses inner compact and outer open approximations for the finitely many remaining regular measures. For every nonnegative simple $g$, $\int g\,dE_\psi=\sum_n\int g\,d(E_n)_{\psi_n}$ by the definition of the sum measure, and [F8] extends this identity to $g(t)=t^2$. By [F5], this second moment is finite exactly when each $\psi_n\in D(T_n)$ and $\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty$, so the domain of $\int t\,dE(t)$ is $D(H_f)$. For $\psi\in D(H_f)$ the bounded truncations $t_R(t):=t\mathbf1_{|t|\le R}$ satisfy $\Phi_E(t_R)=\bigoplus_n\Phi_{E_n}(t_R)$: this follows from the definition of $E$ for simple functions and uniform approximation for bounded Borel functions. As $R\to\infty$, these vectors converge to $(T_n\psi_n)_n$ in norm, first on finitely many sectors by the spectral integral and then on the sector tail using $\sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty$. Therefore $\int t\,dE(t)=H_f$ on precisely $D(H_f)$; regularity and the uniqueness clause of [F5] give $E=E_{H_f}$. For $n=1$, the full-space multiplier PVM of $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ commutes with the transverse projection $M_\Pi$ (scalar multiplication commutes pointwise with $\Pi(k)$), so its restriction to $\mathfrak h$ is a regular PVM. Its scalar second moment is $\int\varepsilon(k)^2\|f(k)\|^2d^3k$, and bounded spectral truncations act as multiplication by $\varepsilon\mathbf1_{\{\varepsilon\le R\}}$, converging in norm on exactly $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})$. Thus its unbounded identity integral is $T_1=\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$, and spectral uniqueness identifies this restricted PVM with $E_1$. The bounded function $h(t):=e^{-\beta t}\mathbf1_{[0,\infty)}(t)$ is $e^{-\beta t}$ on the nonnegative spectrum of every $T_n$; bounded PVM integration is coordinatewise, hence $e^{-\beta H_f}=\bigoplus_ne^{-\beta T_n}$ and its one-particle restriction is $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$.

[Non-compactness of the one-particle multiplier] For $m\ge1$ put $c_m:=2^{-m-2}e_1\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\rho_m:=2^{-m-5}$, and let $\varphi_m$ be a bump as in [F7] with centre $c_m$ and radius $\rho_m$; the balls $B(c_m,\rho_m)$ are pairwise disjoint and contained in $\{|k|\le1/2\}$. Define $g_m:=\Pi\varphi_me_3\in\mathfrak h$; on $B(c_m,\rho_m)$ one has $\Pi(k)e_3=e_3-(k_3/|k|^2)k$ with norm $\sqrt{k_1^2+k_2^2}/|k|\ge|k_1|/|k|\ge(1-\tfrac18)/(1+\tfrac18)>1/2$, so $\|g_m\|\ge\frac12\|\varphi_m\|_2>0$; the $g_m$ have pairwise disjoint supports and hence are pairwise orthogonal. Put $f_m:=g_m/\|g_m\|$; then $(f_m)$ is orthonormal and $|e^{-\beta\varepsilon(k)}|\ge e^{-\beta\alpha}$ on every $B(c_m,\rho_m)$ (since $|k|\le1$ there), so $\|M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}f_m\|_2\ge e^{-\beta\alpha}$ and $\|M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}f_m-M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}f_{m'}\|_2^2=\|Mf_m\|_2^2+\|Mf_{m'}\|_2^2\ge2e^{-2\beta\alpha}$ for $m\ne m'$. The bounded (indeed orthonormal) sequence $(f_m)$ therefore has no subsequence with norm-convergent images, so $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ is not compact by [F6].

[Non-compactness and non-trace-class of $e^{-\beta H_f}$] Suppose $e^{-\beta H_f}$ were compact. The one-particle sector $\operatorname{ran}\Pi_1$ is a closed subspace invariant under $e^{-\beta H_f}$ (by step 4.1 and [F5]); if $(x_m)$ is a bounded sequence in it, compactness in $F(\mathfrak h)$ yields a norm-convergent subsequence of $(e^{-\beta H_f}x_m)$, whose limit lies again in the closed invariant subspace; hence the restriction is compact. By step 5.1 the restriction is $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$, contradicting step 6.1. Therefore $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is not compact; since every trace-class operator is compact ([[def-trace-class-operator]]), it is not trace class. This proves (d).

[Conclusion and scope] Step 2.1 proves (a), step 3.1 proves (b), step 4.1 proves (c), and steps 5.1, 6.1 and 7.1 prove (d). The closing paragraphs of the statement record that the physical photon identification and any thermal interpretation are separate model assumptions, not asserted here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h$ be the transverse space and $H_f=\bigoplus_nT_n$ the free
transverse Fock Hamiltonian of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
and let $A_\pm(g)$, $g\in\mathfrak h$, be the maximal creation and annihilation
operators on $F(\mathfrak h)$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-closed-adjoint-sector-domains]]. Fix a cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ and vectors $g_1,\dots,g_J\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) with
$$\operatorname{supp}g_j\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{g_j}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h,\qquad \varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|,$$
and define the symmetric operator
$$\phi(g):=A_-(g)+A_+(g),\qquad D(\phi(g)):=D(H_f).$$
Let $d\ge1$, let $H_a$ be a Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix, and let
$D_1,\dots,D_J$ be Hermitian $d\times d$ matrices with operator norms
$\|D_j\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then:

(a) for every $\Psi\in D(H_f)$,
$$\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2\le\Bigl\|\frac g{\sqrt\varepsilon}\Bigr\|^2\langle H_f\Psi,\Psi\rangle,\qquad \|A_+(g)\Psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\Psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\Psi\|^2;$$
in particular $\Psi\in D(A_+(g))\cap D(A_-(g))$ and for every $\eta>0$ there is
a finite $C_\eta$ with
$$\|\phi(g)\Psi\|\le\eta\|H_f\Psi\|+C_\eta\|\Psi\| ;$$

(b) $\phi(g)$ is symmetric on $D(H_f)$ and has $H_f$-bound zero
([[def-relative-boundedness-with-respect-to-an-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(c) the free part $H_0:=H_a\otimes I+I\otimes H_f$ with domain
$C^d\otimes D(H_f)$ is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$
([[def-hilbert-space]]); for every $\eta_0\in\mathbb R$ the operator
$$H:=H_0+\eta_0\sum_{j=1}^JD_j\otimes\phi(g_j),\qquad D(H):=C^d\otimes D(H_f),$$
is self-adjoint on $\mathbb C^d\otimes F(\mathfrak h)$ and bounded below
([[thm-kato-rellich]],
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-bounded-fixed-n-operator]] (c)).

The product $D_j\otimes\phi(g_j)$ and the coupling $\eta_0$ carry the dimension
of energy in a physical normalisation; this normalisation is a model choice and
no physical statement about radiation or spontaneous emission is made here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) with completed tensor powers
$H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$, contraction maps
$\Psi_f^{(n)}$, Fock space $F(H)$ and core operators $S_\pm(f)$ on the
finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-creation-contraction-bounds]]. For $f\in H$
define
$$D(A_+(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|P_+^{(n+1)}(f\otimes\psi_n)\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\ (A_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$D(A_-(f)):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(H):\ \sum_{n\in\mathbb N}(n+1)\bigl\|\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\bigr\|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad (A_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1}).$$
Put $D_1:=\{\psi\in F(H):\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$. Then:

(a) $A_+(f)$ and $A_-(f)$ are well-defined linear operators on $F(H)$ with the
displayed domains, and they are the closure and the adjoint of the core operator:
$$A_+(f)=\overline{S_+(f)}=S_-(f)^*,\qquad A_-(f)=S_+(f)^*=\overline{S_-(f)}$$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]],
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);

(b) both $A_\pm(f)$ are closed, densely defined and satisfy
$A_+(f)^*=A_-(f)$, $A_-(f)^*=A_+(f)$; in particular $F_0\subseteq D_1\subseteq D(A_\pm(f))$;

(c) for every $\psi\in D_1$, $\|A_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$ and
$\|A_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1$, where
$\|\psi\|_1^2=\sum_n(n+1)\|\psi_n\|^2$;

(d) for every $g\in H$ and $\psi\in D_1$ the identity
$$\|A_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|A_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2$$
holds.

No boundedness of $A_\pm(f)$ on $F(H)$, no self-adjointness of $A_\pm(f)$, and
no physical interpretation is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with
completed tensor powers $H^{\otimes n}$, symmetric projections $P_+^{(n)}$,
Fock space $F(H)$ and finite-particle space $F_0$ as in
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] and
[[lem-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-fock-sector-projections]].

(a) *Contraction map.* For every $f\in H$ and $n\ge0$ there is a unique bounded
linear map $\Psi_f^{(n)}:H^{\otimes(n+1)}\to H^{\otimes n}$ with
$$\langle\varphi,\Psi_f^{(n)}\chi\rangle=\langle f\otimes\varphi,\chi\rangle \qquad(\varphi\in H^{\otimes n},\ \chi\in H^{\otimes(n+1)})$$
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]); it satisfies
$\|\Psi_f^{(n)}\|\le\|f\|$,
$\Psi_f^{(n)}(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1})=\langle u_1,f\rangle\,u_2\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{n+1}$
on elementary tensors, $\Psi_f^{(n)}(\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n+1)})\subseteq\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$,
and the map $f\mapsto\Psi_f^{(n)}$ is conjugate-linear.

(b) *Creation and annihilation on the core.* Define, for $f\in H$ and
$\psi\in F_0$,
$$(S_+(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt n\,P_+^{(n)}(f\otimes\psi_{n-1})\ (n\ge1),\quad (S_+(f)\psi)_0:=0,$$
$$(S_-(f)\psi)_n:=\sqrt{n+1}\,\Psi_f^{(n)}(\psi_{n+1})\ (n\ge0).$$
Then $S_+(f)\psi,S_-(f)\psi\in F_0$; $S_+(f)$ is linear in $f$ and
$S_-(f)$ is conjugate-linear in $f$; and with
$\|\psi\|_1^2:=\sum_{n}\bigl(n+1\bigr)\|\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for $\psi\in F_0$,
$$\|S_+(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1,\qquad \|S_-(f)\psi\|\le\|f\|\,\|\psi\|_1.$$

(c) *Adjoint relation.* $\langle S_+(f)\varphi,\psi\rangle=\langle\varphi,S_-(f)\psi\rangle$
for all $f\in H$ and $\varphi,\psi\in F_0$
([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]).

(d) *Canonical commutation relation.* For all $f,g\in H$ and $\psi\in F_0$,
$$S_-(f)S_+(g)\psi-S_+(g)S_-(f)\psi=\langle g,f\rangle\,\psi,$$
and consequently
$$\|S_+(g)\psi\|^2=\|S_-(g)\psi\|^2+\|g\|^2\|\psi\|^2.$$

Neither $S_+(f)$ nor $S_-(f)$ is asserted to be bounded on $F(H)$, and no
physical interpretation (particle creation, radiation or measurement) is
asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, the Axiom of Dependent Choice and the
Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]],
[[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix a parameter $\alpha>0$, define the transverse
subspace
$$\mathfrak h:=\Bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3):\ k\cdot f(k)=0\ \text{for a.e. }k\Bigr\}$$
with the $L^2$ inner product, define the bounded multiplier-valued function
$\Pi(k):=\mathrm{id}-|k|^{-2}kk^{\mathsf T}$ for $k\ne0$ and $\Pi(0):=0$, and let
$M_\Pi$ be multiplication by $\Pi$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$
([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Write
$\varepsilon(k):=\alpha|k|$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be multiplication by
$\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}:=M_\varepsilon|_{\mathfrak h}$.
Let $F(\mathfrak h)$ be the Fock space of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-hilbert-direct-sum-construction]] with sectors
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and for $n\ge1$ define
$$T_n\psi:=\varepsilon_n\psi,\quad \varepsilon_n(k_1,\dots,k_n):=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha|k_i|,\qquad D(T_n):=\{\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}:\varepsilon_n\psi\in\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}\},$$
and $T_0:=0$ on $\mathbb C$. Finally put
$$H_f:=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}T_n,\qquad D(H_f):=\Bigl\{\psi\in F(\mathfrak h):\ \psi_n\in D(T_n)\text{ for every }n,\ \sum_n\|T_n\psi_n\|^2<\infty\Bigr\}.$$
Then:

(a) $\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_\Pi$ is a closed separable subspace of
$L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$, invariant under $M_\varepsilon$, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h}$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on
$\mathfrak h$ with $D(\varepsilon_{\mathfrak h})=\{f\in\mathfrak h:\varepsilon f\in\mathfrak h\}$
([[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]],
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]], [[def-separable-space]]);

(b) each $T_n$ is a positive self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ with the displayed domain
([[def-hilbert-space]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-euclidean-l2-product-unitary]],
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]);

(c) $H_f$ is self-adjoint and positive with domain $D(H_f)$; it commutes with
every sector projection $\Pi_n$ (i.e. $T_n$ maps its sector into itself);

(d) for every $\beta>0$ the bounded operator $e^{-\beta H_f}$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]],
[[def-projection-valued-measure]]) is not compact and in particular not trace
class ([[def-compact-linear-operator]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]); more
precisely its restriction to the one-particle sector equals the multiplication
operator $M_{e^{-\beta\varepsilon}}$ on $\mathfrak h$, which is not compact, and
the restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact.

The identification of $\mathfrak h$, $\varepsilon$ and $H_f$ with physical
transverse photons in a chosen frame is a separate model assumption and is not
asserted here; no thermal interpretation of $e^{-\beta H_f}$ is claimed either.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), let $a,b\ge1$, and let $\lambda_n$ denote Lebesgue measure on $\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ as defined in [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and completed from Borel measure as in [[cor-lebesgue-sigma-algebra-is-the-completion-of-borel-lebesgue-measure]]. The product measure $\lambda_a\times\lambda_b$ exists by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]], and under $\mathbb R^{a+b}=\mathbb R^a\times\mathbb R^b$, $\lambda_{a+b}$ is its completion ([[thm-euclidean-lebesgue-measure-is-the-completion-of-the-product-of-lebesgue-measures]]). Write $H_a=L^2(\mathbb R^a,\lambda_a)$ and $H_b=L^2(\mathbb R^b,\lambda_b)$, with $L^2$ understood as the almost-everywhere quotient of square-integrable measurable functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). Then there is a unique linear isometry

$$\Theta:H_a\widehat\otimes H_b\longrightarrow L^2(\mathbb R^{a+b})$$

with $\Theta(f\otimes g)(x,y)=f(x)g(y)$ for all $f\in H_a$, $g\in H_b$ and a.e. $(x,y)$, and $\Theta$ is onto: it is a surjective linear isometry, hence unitary. Vector-valued or spin factors follow by finite component sums. No identification of non-Euclidean product measures is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$, and set
$U(t):=e^{itT}=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{it\lambda}\,dE(\lambda)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$.
Then $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group,
$U(t)D(T)=D(T)$ and $TU(t)=U(t)T$ on $D(T)$, and the derivative
$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(U(t)x-x)$ exists exactly for $x\in D(T)$, where it equals
$iTx$. Thus the generator of $U$ is $G=iT$, with $D(G)=D(T)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, and let $f,g:\Omega\to X$ be Bochner integrable ([[def-bochner-integrable-function]]) with $\alpha,\beta$ scalars. Then $\alpha f+\beta g$ is Bochner integrable and $\int_\Omega(\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int_\Omega f\,d\mu+\beta\int_\Omega g\,d\mu$; for a measurable set $E$ the same identity holds with $f,g$ replaced by $f\mathbf 1_E,g\mathbf 1_E$. The integral is therefore additive and homogeneous, and in particular well defined on differences.

derivations.claim: [Free flow and vertex bounds] Diagonalizing the finite Hermitian $H_a$ and using [F3], [F4] gives $U_0(t)=e^{itH_a/\hbar}\otimes e^{itH_f/\hbar}$. Thus $U_0(t)$ preserves each $\mathcal K_m$, commutes with $F$ on $\mathcal G$, and is isometric and strongly continuous for the graph norm: both $U_0(t)x$ and $FU_0(t)x=U_0(t)Fx$ are continuous. On $\mathcal K_m$, the finite-sector extension of $B$ from [F2] satisfies $\|Bx\|\le|\eta_0|\gamma\sqrt{m+1}\|x\|$ and takes values in $\mathcal K_{m+1}$. Its free conjugate therefore satisfies $\|V(t)x\|\le|\eta_0|\gamma\sqrt{m+1}\|x\|$. The factor $|\eta_0|$ is included exactly once in this bound; $\gamma$ and $C$ contain no coupling.

[Cutoff commutator and graph-domain extension] For $g$ supported in $\{0<\varepsilon\le\Lambda\}$, $\varepsilon g\in\mathfrak h$ and $\|\varepsilon g\|\le\Lambda\|g\|$. On symmetric elementary tensors with factors in $D(\varepsilon)$, the sector multiplier and creation formula give $[H_f,A_+(g)]=A_+(\varepsilon g)$. For contraction the removed factor contributes $-\langle\varepsilon u,g\rangle=-\langle u,\varepsilon g\rangle$, so $[H_f,A_-(g)]=-A_-(\varepsilon g)$. These identities extend to every finite-photon graph vector, with no claim that all of $F_0$ lies in $D(H_f)$. Indeed, in sector $n$ first cut each mode to $\varepsilon\le R$; dominated convergence in the Euclidean representation [F3] gives convergence of both the vector and its energy multiplier. On that cutoff subspace, energy is bounded by $nR$, so finite sums of elementary cutoff tensors, symmetrized, approximate in graph norm by tensor density. This supplies a graph core in each $\mathcal G_m$. The field and its candidate commutator are bounded on $\mathcal K_m$ by [F2], with respective bounds $2\sqrt{m+1}\|g\|$ and $2\Lambda\sqrt{m+1}\|g\|$. Applying the core identity to a graph-approximating sequence makes the output and its energy image converge; closedness of $H_f$ proves graph-domain preservation and the identity on the limit. Hence for $x\in\mathcal G_m$, $Bx\in\mathcal G_{m+1}$ and $$FBx=BFx+Q_Bx,\qquad Q_B:=\eta_0\sum_jD_j\otimes\bigl(A_+(\varepsilon g_j)-A_-(\varepsilon g_j)\bigr),\qquad \|Q_Bx\|\le|\eta_0|\gamma\Lambda\sqrt{m+1}\|x\|.$$

[Conjugated commutator and graph continuity] Since $F$ commutes with $U_0(t)$, step 1.2 gives on $\mathcal G_m$ $$FV(t)x=V(t)Fx+Q(t)x,\qquad Q(t):=U_0(t)Q_BU_0(-t),$$ with $\|Q(t)x\|\le|\eta_0|\gamma\Lambda\sqrt{m+1}\|x\|$. The conjugations in $Q(t)$ are retained. Equivalently, the sector formulas give $D_j(t)=e^{itH_a/\hbar}D_je^{-itH_a/\hbar}$ and $g_j(t)=e^{it\varepsilon/\hbar}g_j$, with $$V(t)=\eta_0\sum_jD_j(t)\otimes\phi(g_j(t)),\qquad Q(t)=\eta_0\sum_jD_j(t)\otimes\bigl(A_+(\varepsilon g_j(t))-A_-(\varepsilon g_j(t))\bigr).$$ The same positive phase occurs in the annihilation vector argument because that argument is conjugate-linear, as in [F2]. The resulting graph bound is $$\|V(t)x\|_{\mathcal G}\le|\eta_0|\gamma\sqrt{m+1}\bigl(\|Fx\|+(1+\Lambda)\|x\|\bigr).$$ Thus $V(t):\mathcal G_m\to\mathcal G_{m+1}$ is uniformly bounded in $t$ for these graph norms. Strong graph continuity of $U_0$, the fixed graph-bounded $B$ between these spaces, and the expression $U_0(t)BU_0(-t)x$ show that $t\mapsto V(t)x$ is graph continuous. On the full $\mathcal G$, [F1] and the graph isometry of $U_0$ additionally give $\|V(t)x\|\le K\|x\|_{\mathcal G}$ for one finite $K$ independent of $t$, and strong continuity as a map $\mathcal G\to\mathcal K$. No global map $V(t):\mathcal G\to\mathcal G$ is asserted.

[Chronological products and their graph bounds] Define $P_n(t_1,\ldots,t_n):=V(t_n)\cdots V(t_1)\Psi_0$, with $P_0=\Psi_0$. At the $k$-th vertex, the earlier product is in $\mathcal G_{k-1}$, so steps 1.1 and 2.1 give a factor $|\eta_0|\gamma\sqrt k$ in its Hilbert bound. Consequently $P_n\in\mathcal G_n$ and $\|P_n\|\le(|\eta_0|\gamma)^n\sqrt{n!}$. The graph commutator gives recursively $\|FP_k\|\le|\eta_0|\gamma\sqrt k(\|FP_{k-1}\|+\Lambda\|P_{k-1}\|)$; since $F\Psi_0=0$, induction yields $\|FP_n\|\le n\Lambda(|\eta_0|\gamma)^n\sqrt{n!}$. Each product is jointly continuous in its time variables for the graph norm: at each stage use strong graph continuity of the next $V$ on a fixed vector and its uniform graph bound to control the changing previous vector. For $n=0$ the Hilbert bound is $1$ and the energy bound is $0$, including when $|\eta_0|\gamma=0$.

[Graph Bochner terms and the genuine recurrence] The graph space $\mathcal G$ is Banach: a graph-Cauchy sequence has limits of both the vectors and their $F$ images in the Hilbert space, and closedness of $F$ identifies them as a graph limit. Each $\mathcal G_n$ is closed in it. Step 3.1 and [F5] therefore make every iterated chronological integral a Bochner integral in $\mathcal G_n$. Its graph and Hilbert norm bounds follow by integrating the preceding product bounds over the simplex; the volume is $t^n/n!$, obtained recursively from $\int_0^t s^{n-1}/(n-1)!\,ds=t^n/n!$. Each factor of the integral contributes $1/\hbar$, giving $$\|\Psi_n(t)\|\le\frac{(|\eta_0|Ct)^n}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad \|F\Psi_n(t)\|\le\frac{n\Lambda(|\eta_0|Ct)^n}{\sqrt{n!}}.$$ For $n=0$ these bounds mean $1$ and $0$. Integrating the latest vertex last gives the actual left-vertex recurrence $$\Psi_{n+1}(t)=\frac1{i\hbar}\int_0^tV(s)\Psi_n(s)\,ds.$$ For fixed $s$, move $V(s)$ through the inner integral as a bounded linear map $\mathcal G_n\to\mathcal G_{n+1}$ by [F5]; the earlier vertices have times below $s$, with $V(s)$ on the left. This also proves graph continuity of each term, and proves (a) and graph-domain membership in (b).

[Uniform graph convergence] Fix $T<\infty$ and put $a:=|\eta_0|CT$. The graph majorant is $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n\Lambda)a^n/\sqrt{n!}$. For $a>0$ the ratio of consecutive scalar terms tends to zero: it is $a(1+(n+1)\Lambda)/((1+n\Lambda)\sqrt{n+1})$. It is eventually at most $1/2$, proving convergence by a geometric tail comparison. If $a=0$, every positive-order term is zero and only the zeroth term remains. Thus the series converges uniformly for $0\le t\le T$ in the Banach graph space, and its sum $\Psi(t)$ is graph continuous and belongs to $D(H)=\mathcal G$.

[Integral equation and Hilbert derivative] The uniform bound $\|V(s)x\|\le K\|x\|_{\mathcal G}$ from step 2.1 makes $V(s)\sum_{n\le M}\Psi_n(s)$ converge uniformly in Hilbert norm on $[0,T]$ to $V(s)\Psi(s)$. This limiting curve is continuous by graph continuity of $\Psi$, strong continuity of $V:\mathcal G\to\mathcal K$, and the same uniform bound. Sum the recurrences of step 4.1 and use the Bochner norm inequality [F5] to pass to the limit in their Hilbert integrals. The result is $\Psi(t)=\Psi_0+(i\hbar)^{-1}\int_0^tV(s)\Psi(s)\,ds$. The Banach-valued fundamental theorem now gives $\Psi\in C^1([0,T];\mathcal K)$, with the right derivative at zero, and $i\hbar\Psi'(t)=V(t)\Psi(t)$, $\Psi(0)=\Psi_0$. Along with step 5.1 this proves (b); graph continuity is used for domain control, while the differential equation is a Hilbert-space derivative.

[Identification with the self-adjoint dynamics] Put $Y(t):=U_0(-t)\Psi(t)$. It is graph continuous and belongs to $D(H)$. The difference quotient splits into the difference of the free group on the fixed domain vector $\Psi(t)$ and the free group times the difference quotient of $\Psi$, so [F4] and step 6.1 justify the product derivative in Hilbert norm. Thus $i\hbar Y'=H_0Y+U_0(-t)V(t)\Psi=H_0Y+BY=HY$ and $Y(0)=\Psi_0$. By [F1], [F4], the Stone curve $e^{-itH/\hbar}\Psi_0$ is another strong domain-valued solution because $\Psi_0\in\mathcal G=D(H)$. For their difference $w$, symmetry of $H$ gives $$\frac d{dt}\|w(t)\|^2=2\operatorname{Re}\langle w'(t),w(t)\rangle=2\operatorname{Re}\left(-\frac i\hbar\langle Hw(t),w(t)\rangle\right)=0.$$ Both initial values agree, so $w=0$, proving (c) for every finite $t\ge0$.

[Tail, vacuum and zero branches] By step 7.1 and unitarity, the truncation error at time $t$ equals in norm the interaction-picture tail, so it is at most $\sum_{n\ge N}(|\eta_0|Ct)^n/\sqrt{n!}$; for $0\le t\le T$ this is at most the stated $T$ tail, proving (d). The vacuum zeroth term has $F\Psi_0=0$ and norm one. At $t=0$ all positive-order integrals vanish. If $\eta_0=0$, or if $\gamma=0$ (all contributing $D_j$ or $g_j$ zero), then $B=V=0$, all positive-order terms vanish, the interaction-picture sum is exactly $\Psi_0$, and the tail is zero for every $N\ge1$. The argument supplies finite-time convergence and the actual self-adjoint evolution, with the original scope limitations retained.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on $(X,\Sigma)$,
and for $x,y\in H$ define

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad E_{x,y}(B):=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle \qquad(B\in\Sigma).$$

Then:

1. $E_x$ is a positive measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ with $E_x(X)=\|x\|^2$ and
   $0\le E_x(B)\le\|x\|^2$ for every $B$;
2. $E_{x,y}$ is a finite complex measure on $(X,\Sigma)$, the map
   $(x,y)\mapsto E_{x,y}$ is linear in $x$ and conjugate-linear in $y$, and
   $E_{y,x}=\overline{E_{x,y}}$, meaning $E_{y,x}(B)=\overline{E_{x,y}(B)}$ for
   every $B$;
3. $|E_{x,y}|(X)\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $|E_{x,y}(B)|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$ for every
   $B$, and the polarization identity
   $$E_{x,y}=\frac14\sum_{k=0}^{3}i^kE_{x+i^ky}$$
   holds as an identity of complex measures, where $i^k$ are the fourth roots
   of unity $1,i,-1,-i$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.
